items.title: Ford's $5 day was a retention crisis fix, not generosity
items.claim: In January 1914, Henry Ford doubled the basic wage at his Highland Park plant to $5 a day. What problem was he solving?

options.text: Falling demand for the Model T
Catastrophic worker turnover — the assembly line was so monotonous that annual turnover had reached around 370%, meaning the plant had to hire roughly 50,000 people to maintain a workforce of 14,000
A unionisation drive he wanted to prevent

items.reveal:
Daniel Raff and Lawrence Summers's 1987 paper analysed Ford's wage decision. Turnover collapsed after the announcement; absenteeism dropped from 10% to 2.5%; productivity rose. The wage was conditional — there was a 'Sociological Department' that inspected workers' homes for 'good moral character' to qualify.

The popular story (Ford paid workers enough to buy his cars) is a post-hoc rationalisation. A Model T cost roughly $440; a workforce of 14,000 buying cars wouldn't move the market.

The wage was efficient: Ford gained productivity worth more than the extra wage bill.
items.why: Famous 'visionary' business decisions usually have boring, specific operational drivers. The $5 day looks like generosity; it was wage-efficiency arbitrage.

items.title: Most mergers and acquisitions destroy shareholder value
items.claim: Multiple long-run studies of M&A outcomes (KPMG, Bain, Harvard Business Review reviews) report what share of deals fail to create value for the acquiring firm's shareholders?
items.reveal:
KPMG's recurring M&A studies, Bain & Company's analyses, and Roger Martin's 2016 HBR piece 'M&A: The One Thing You Need to Get Right' all converge: 70-90% of acquisitions fail to deliver the anticipated synergies, often because the acquirer overpays.

Specific failures: AOL-Time Warner (2000, $165bn), Daimler-Chrysler (1998), Quaker-Snapple (1994), Microsoft-Nokia (2014). The 'winner's curse' (Thaler, 1988) explains why competitive bidding tends to produce winners who overestimated.

Organic growth tends to deliver more predictable returns but at a slower pace.
items.why: M&A is one of the most-used growth strategies and one of the worst-performing. The gap between expected and actual synergies is systematically positive.

items.title: High gearing is risk, not failure
items.claim: A firm has long-term debt of £40 million and equity of £60 million. Its gearing ratio (debt / debt+equity) is 40%. Which statement is most accurate?

options.text: Gearing this high is always dangerous
Higher gearing magnifies returns to shareholders in good times and losses in bad — utilities routinely run 60%+ because cash flows are stable
Equity is always cheaper than debt

items.reveal:
UK water and electricity utilities (Severn Trent, National Grid) often carry gearing above 60% because regulated cash flows make debt servicing predictable. Tech firms (pre-2022) often had near-zero gearing because cash flows were volatile and equity was cheap.

Modigliani and Miller (1958) argued that, in perfect markets, capital structure is irrelevant. In real markets — with taxes, bankruptcy costs and asymmetric information — there is an optimal range. Lehman Brothers' gearing reached above 30:1 (debt:equity) before its 2008 collapse.
items.why: Whether high gearing is reckless depends on what cash flows look like. The number alone tells you little.
